It breaks over uneven reef and sand, and its closeness to San José makes it one of the easier quality points in the country to reach. facts.name: Cahuita
facts.windOffshore: SW (surfnerd wind exposure S - W, "Offshore from SW")
hazards: Watch the rip, which can run a bit, and keep the reef in mind at the point. (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Cahuita is a stretch of black sand beach break inside Cahuita National Park, with a fun left-hand reef and point tucked into one end. That mix gives you rights and lefts in the same session, breaking over sand at the beach and reef and sand at the point. It is one of the better options on the Caribbean side of Costa Rica, a coast with real charm and a handful of quality waves, and a good call if you happen to be in the country during the Pacific's offseason. Sightseeing and surfing in one spot works nicely here. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): Park at the entrance to Cahuita National Park or on the side of the main beach road, then walk down to the black sand beach.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Colorado is a river-mouth beachbreak on Nicaragua's Pacific coast, breaking over sandbars that the river keeps constantly replenished. It's regarded as one of the country's best beachbreaks when it comes together, throwing fast, hollow barrels with both lefts and rights on offer. The rights tend to be the hollower of the two, while the lefts run racey and rippable. The peak can shift around, which helps spread surfers across a few different takeoff spots. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Colorado: "Playa Colorado in Tola Province is an exposed river break that has very consistent surf Ideal winds are from the northeast. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. The river breaks offer lefts and rights. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of - Private beach." Access (surfnerd): Staying at the neighbouring Hacienda Iguana gives the easiest access. Otherwise you'll need to boat in or hike in, and parking nearby is restricted. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Colorado 0.2 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: El Paredón is a black-sand beachbreak sitting on the east side of the Canal de Chiquimulilla, in a fishing community where a handful of surf camps have set up shop. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Take care of the strong rips here." Access (surfnerd): The community has camping and a surf school on hand. facts.name: El Transito
facts.facing: WSW (surfnerd el-transito-2: "Faces WSW"); WSW (surfnerd el-transito: "Faces WSW")
facts.windOffshore: ENE (surfnerd wind exposure NNE - ESE, "Offshore from ENE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: El Transito sits in a crescent-shaped cove and vacuums up whatever swell is around, feeding it onto sandbars that never stop moving. Reef protrusions at either end refract the swell into multiple peaks, and a few rocks sit scattered just outside the takeoff zone. The bottom is mostly sand with patches of uneven reef, and it throws both lefts and rights. The wave itself is mellow, with softer barrel sections and medium-length rides that suit everyone, though it gets a lot less friendly once it pushes overhead and starts closing out. Day to day it's often just an average wave, but it has its good days, and the water is usually clean. Surfnerd lists this break 2 times (el-transito-2, el-transito); merged. Second Surfnerd entry https://www.surfnerd.com/surf-forecast/el-transito: workable swell S - SW (Best from SW), 2ft - 8ft, Uneven Reef, Point, Left, Low, Mid, High, Intermediate. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): Getting here is easy. It's close to Managua with one road running straight in from the highway, and you can park for free on the roadside. Other guide pins from this position: surfnerd el-transito 0.5 km.

facts.name: El Zonte
facts.windOffshore: N (surfnerd wind exposure NW - NE, "Offshore from N"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind"); North-northeast (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Mid, High (surfnerd); There is a left hand reef break Best around high tide when the tide is rising. (surf-forecast)
hazards: rips and rocks (surf-forecast)
As with most points, there's a bit of current to deal with. (surfnerd)
facts.season: Spring, Summer, Autumn (surfnerd); Winter, most often November (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: El Zonte is a river mouth and rocky point in the sleepy town of the same name, a short drive from Sunzal. The main draw is a long, predictable right-hander that peels down the boulders, staying rippable when it's small and turning hollow as the swell builds. When it gets big enough, some sucky lefts open up on the other side of the bay. It carries a mellower feel than the other nearby breaks. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast El-Zonte: "El Zonte in Costa del Balsamo is an exposed reef,point and rivermouth break that has very consistent surf Ideal winds are from the north northeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the south southwest. There is a left hand reef break Best around high tide when the tide is rising. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Camping and surf schools have grown up around the town, making it easy to base yourself nearby and make the short paddle out. Parking is free, including roadside spots. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast El-Zonte 0.8 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Hog Hole is the outside point in a string of three quality right-hand point and reef breaks around Cabo Matapalo. It gets wild and heavy when the swell is big, with a nasty inside mix of ledges, boulders and cobblestone, so it rewards surfers who know how to read a serious point. Check: surfnerd states facing SE but best swell SW (90 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Hog-Hole: "Hog Hole in Golfo Dulce is an exposed reef and point break that has very consistent waves Works best in offshore winds from the north northwest. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the south. It very rarely gets crowded here. Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Getting here takes some effort. The 4x4 dirt roads into Cabo Matapalo are easily cut off by swollen rivers, and the accommodation options nearby are limited and expensive. Parking is restricted. facts.name: La Barra - Likin
facts.windOffshore: NNW (surfnerd wind exposure WNW - NNE, "Offshore from NNW"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind")
hazards: Tide is the thing to get right here: river flow throws up hectic rips on dropping tides, so time your session for low incoming or slack high, and on big swells even dead high is a good window. (surfnerd)
It can work across low, mid, and high, but a rising tide is the better call and keeps you clear of the killer rip. (surfnerd)
The sucky take-off and current make it a genuine struggle for beginners, and there are easier beachbreaks nearby if that's the level you're at. (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: La Barra is a hollow rivermouth and jetty setup at Balneario Likin, 5km (3mi) past Puerto San Jose on the longest stretch of coastal road in Guatemala, where you can check several beaches without really leaving the highway. The surf here ranks among the best in the country. The righthander is often long and predictable, with hollow pockets broken up by slashable shoulders, and it stays rideable until slightly overhead. The left off the peak sucks hard and runs straight at the rocky tip of the jetty, so it often closes out. Shifting sandbars keep changing the shape and quality, so what you find one session may not be what you get the next. Check: surfnerd states facing SSE but best swell SW (67.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): There's a surf camp close by, plus camping, a surf school and a surf shop. Balneario Likin itself is one of the country's only high-end coastal resorts.

facts.name: La Bocana
facts.windOffshore: N (surfnerd wind exposure NW - NE, "Offshore from N"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: La Bocana is the Libertad area's only genuine lefthander, tucked at the south end of the little village of El Tunco. It breaks where the Rio Grande rivermouth meets the sea, an open, cobblestone-lined "bocana" that acts as a swell magnet and almost always has something to ride. The wave is punchier and harder to maneuver than its neighbor Sunzal: a steep drop into a couple of good sections and a dredging inside barrel. The bottom is a mix of rocks and sand. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Access (surfnerd): The bus from La Libertad takes about half an hour and costs less than a dollar. You'll find free, paid, and roadside parking nearby.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: La Paz is the inside section of Punta Roca, the nearly half-mile-long cobble and boulder righthander at La Libertad. It's an easier, less critical wave than the top of the point, breaking over cobbles, boulders, and patches of uneven reef and sand. When a big swell is running it can turn excellent, throwing the occasional kegging right, and it sits closer in and less crowded than the main peak. The inside doesn't offer everything Punta Roca does, but it's a genuinely good wave and you can pick off a few nice ones. Many surfers paddle out here and make the trek up the point by water. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the west northwest. Waves at the beach break both left and right and there are also left and right hand reef breaks on offer.. When the surf is up, crowds are likely Take care of ." Access (surfnerd): Parking is a tiny public lot with around ten spaces roughly 200 meters from the break, plus some roadside parking, and it's free either way. Condos and the private Barcelo resort block other access, so a taxi is the easy option if you're not staying in Langosta. Keep an eye out for shallow rocks in places, and note the rivermouth can carry polluted runoff. Relatively few surfers here, even on good days. Take care of the strong rips here." Access (surfnerd): Getting here means a long drive in on the inland freeway, which is a big part of why it stays so uncrowded. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Las-Lisas 4.7 km.

facts.name: Mal Pais
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); Northeast (surf-forecast)
facts.season: Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter (surfnerd); Winter, most often December (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Mal Pais sits at the southwest tip of the rugged Nicoya Peninsula, sharing a stretch of coast with neighbouring Playa Carmen and Santa Teresa. The waves are shifty A-frames with long walls that run on before folding into inside closeouts, and there's enough beach here to spread a lot of surfers out. It's an easy, almost California-style beachbreak, more fun than heavy, and it breaks over sand with some scattered rocks. Head north and it tends to get bigger and hollower, particularly on a south swell, while the stretch south towards the Cabo Blanco Nature Preserve holds a few quirky, bigger-wave reefbreaks. There are semi-secret spots waiting further north too. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Mal-Pais-Santa-Teresa: "Mal Pais in Golfo de Nicoya is an exposed reef break that is often working Works best in offshore winds from the northeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. Rarely crowded here. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here." Access (surfnerd): If you're not staying right on the beach, a handful of dirt trails run off the road down to the sand north of Frank's Place. Pick one, and lock up your stuff before you paddle out. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Mal-Pais-Santa-Teresa 8.2 km.

facts.name: Matapalo
facts.windOffshore: NW (surfnerd wind exposure W - N, "Offshore from NW"); North-northwest (surf-forecast)

facts.season: Spring, Autumn, Winter (surfnerd); Summer, most often May (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Matapalo is a right-hander on the Osa Peninsula, just south of Drake's Bay and across the Golfo Dulce from the world-class left at Pavones. It isn't one wave but a scattered series of them, breaking over sand and rock as a mix of reef and point. Three named breaks sit along this stretch: Cabo Matapalo, Backwash and Pan Dulce, each moody in its own way, with quality and size shifting from one swell to the next. It can be inconsistent, but when the setup lines up it delivers genuine right-hand bliss, and the water here is beautiful. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Cabo-Matapalo: "Cabo Matapalo in Golfo Dulce is an exposed point break that has very consistent surf Offshore winds are from the north northwest. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): A 4x4-only road runs down to a beachside campsite, with sparse accommodation in the area. Most people park along the road and follow a winding trail out to the three breaks. A few private houses have started blocking road access to Pan Dulce, but you can still walk in along the beach. Hiring a boat from Pavones is another way in. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Cabo-Matapalo 0.3 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Nosara is a sand-bottomed beachbreak on the Guanacaste Coast of Costa Rica's Nicoya Peninsula, throwing both rights and lefts along a long stretch of open beach. The town carries the name, but the surf itself happens at Playa Guiones, where a couple of miles of coast give you several peaks to pick from. Some sections break over rock and take on a canyon-like shape, and the whole setup rates as reliably fun with days that turn out quite good. Surfnerd lists this break 2 times (nosara, playa-nosara); merged. Second Surfnerd entry https://www.surfnerd.com/surf-forecast/playa-nosara: workable swell S - NW (Best from SW), 2ft - 6ft, Sand, Beach, Left, Right, Low, Mid, High, Beginner. Ideal winds are from the north northeast. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the west northwest. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of ." Access (surfnerd): At the end of the road you'll find an informal lot, and plenty of people just pull over on the roadside instead. The first 50 meters back from the sand have been left undeveloped to protect the coastline, so the walk in stays short and the beach stays open. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Pan Dulce is a right-hand point tucked inside the Golfo, and it's a seriously beautiful place to surf. When a south swell fills in with some size, it turns into a Rincon-style point with long, mellow cutback shoulders and zippy walls that are perfect for longboarding. It often breaks as two separate sections over an uneven reef-and-sand bottom, and there's an inside beachbreak that's ideal for beginners finding their feet. Check: surfnerd states facing ESE but best swell SW (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Pan-Dulce: "Pan Dulce in Golfo Dulce is an exposed point break that is usually a safe bet The best wind direction is from the north northwest. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the south. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): There's camping at the spot, plus free roadside parking. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Pan-Dulce 0.6 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Panga Drops is a horseshoe-shaped reef at the north end of Playa Iguanas, a fun alternative to the heavier Colorados next door. The bombora-style setup picks up almost everything on offer and throws out whizzing walls, inside barrels, and fading shoulders that shift around a big playing field. Both lefts and rights peel here, and on a proper swell they can barrel. When it's on, it's a genuinely good wave. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): Base yourself at Iguanas for the easiest access. Otherwise you'll need to boat or hike in, and walking from Gigante or taking a boat also spares you the long paddle out. Parking is restricted.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Pavones serves up some of the longest left-hand rides on the planet, peeling down a point of sand and boulders close to shore. On a solid south swell, rides of up to a kilometre and around three minutes are possible, and it's full-on down-the-line surfing that stretches your bottom turns and top turns far longer than usual. When it's on, it ranks among the best waves anywhere, a run of connected sections that shape and pace all the way down the point. The top of the point, west of the rivermouth, is the main takeoff zone. Check: surfnerd states facing WNW but best swell S (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Pavones: "Pavones in Golfo Dulce is a sheltered point break that has unreliable waves The best wind direction is from the east. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Take care of rocks in the line up." Access (surfnerd): The spot sits right behind the soccer field, with camping nearby and free roadside parking. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Bonita is the main beach in Costa Rica's Limón area, and its standout is a left reef that breaks over dead coral. The chunky left reef at the north end turns hollow and slamming when the swell fills in. There's also a high-tide beachbreak that tends to close out around head-high, plus short, sucky Los Tumbos rights at low tide over a rocky bottom that bodyboarders favour. A 1991 earthquake lifted the local coral reefs by a couple of feet, part of what shaped these Limón breaks. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Playa-Bonita: "Playa Bonita in Limon is an exposed reef break that has pretty consitent surf The best wind direction is from the south southwest. Most of the surf comes fis in the form of windswells and the best wave direction is from the northeast. A left hand reef break. Sometimes crowded. Take care of rips,jellyfish and coral." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Playa-Bonita 1.4 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Conchalio is a mile-long stretch of sand and rock-bottom peaks just up the road from La Libertad. The peaks break both right and left over a sand bottom, and when they line up they are speedy, thumping and full of barrels. It is a tricky one to score, and the wave quality is a long way off El Salvador's world-class points, but it is always worth a check on flat days. Closeouts are the main thing to watch for. Surfnerd has 2 entries for this break with different stated facings (playa-conchalio-la-libertad-department=SSW, playa-conchalio=S); seaward uses the primary entry (playa-conchalio-la-libertad-department), both kept. Second Surfnerd entry https://www.surfnerd.com/surf-forecast/playa-conchalio: workable swell S - W (Best from W), 2ft - 6ft, Sand, Beach, Left, Right, Mid, High, Beginner. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Access (surfnerd): Getting in is easy. The beach sits just off the highway west of La Libertad. This is a fairly local stretch of coastline with only a few small hotels and hostels, and that thin tourism infrastructure is part of the appeal if you want some culture with your surf trip. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Esterillos is a south-facing stretch of coast where patches of reef mix into a small sand bay and then open out into miles of beachbreak. Esterillos Oeste holds a wide range of waves, from beginner-friendly peaks to serious ones, and its A-frames are shaped by a combination of sandbars and reef. That mix keeps things moving: one peak fades as the tide shifts while a differently shaped one wakes up a couple hundred yards away, so conditions change fast and local knowledge counts for a lot. Worth knowing there are two Esterillos, Este and Oeste. Both are fairly average day to day but can genuinely shine when the stars align. At the northwest end of the beach, several reefs break calmly enough that longboarders get rides from the outside all the way through to the shorepound. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Esterillos-Oeste: "Esterillos Oeste in Golfo de Nicoya is an exposed beach break that has pretty consitent surf Offshore winds blow from the north. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the south. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Watch out for rocks." Access (surfnerd): Park at the beach and walk from there. Numerous spots are within walking distance. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Guiones is the main beach at Nosara and one of Costa Rica's most forgiving black-sand beachbreaks. It's a long, wide stretch of sand with plenty of room to spread out, and the waves here are famously easy and safe. Even when it jumps to double overhead, there are no real beatdowns to fear: the thickest lips just spin you around and pop you out the back, and the black sand makes duck-diving painless. On a good day it runs like a skate park, with enough speed and push to keep things fun and minimal consequences if it goes wrong. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Guiones: "Guiones (Playa Nosara) in Guanacaste is an exposed beach break that has consistent surf Works best in offshore winds from the east northeast. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the west northwest. The beach break provides left and right handers. Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, crowds are likely Watch out for sharks." Access (surfnerd): Getting in is simple: walk down one of the many access paths in town. There's camping nearby. Like much of the region, Guiones sees its share of petty theft, so keep your valuables locked up and out of sight. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Guiones 1.0 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Hermosa is a powerful beachbreak spread along four miles of scalloped black sand in Costa Rica. The peaks shift constantly, throwing up A-frames that break both left and right over a sand bottom, and the wave carries serious punch — on double-overhead days it can close out and intimidate. A strong side current runs the length of the beach, so it rarely sits still. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Playa-Hermosa: "Playa Hermosa in Golfo de Nicoya is an exposed beach break that is usually a safe bet Offshore winds blow from the northeast. Surfing here means negotiating dangerous rips." Access (surfnerd): Getting there is easy: it's about a two-hour drive from the airport. You'll find camping, a surf school, and a surf shop nearby, plus a car park with free parking and roadside spots. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Playa-Hermosa 0.1 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa Hermosa South is a black-sand beachbreak with a reputation as the most consistent one in Costa Rica. Four miles of scalloped sand and fairly deep water offshore leave it open to just about any swell except northwest, and the shifting A-frames peel both right and left. A strong side current runs the length of it, which is part of why you can usually find an uncrowded peak somewhere along the stretch. At size it turns genuinely heavy, though it has an annoying tendency to close out once it pushes past double-overhead. The bottom is shallow, so snapped boards and long hold-downs come with the territory, but that's a small price to pay for a green, spinning tube with jungled coastline as the view. The water is surprisingly clean for somewhere this close to a populated area. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate, Expert. Access (surfnerd): Getting here is easy: about a two-hour drive from the airport and you're right there. Park at one of the many restaurants, bars or hotels along the beach.

Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Watch out for sea-lice etc." Surf-forecast Jaco-Beach: "Jaco Beach in Golfo de Nicoya is an exposed beach break that is often working and works all around the year. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Playa San Diego is a wide swath of coconut palm-fringed black sand beach southeast of La Libertad, on the road that leads toward Punta Roca and the rest of El Salvador's southeast coast. It's quieter than La Libertad and less touristy than El Tunco, and the sandbanks out front occasionally throw up brilliant A-frames. As a beachbreak it doesn't rate as highly as the famous points nearby, and closeouts are part of the deal, but it's a pleasant, authentic slice of Salvadorian coast that's worth a look, especially when the pointbreaks are on the small side. It also makes a good home base, with well-reviewed hotels and hostels and a variety of restaurants close by. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Playa-San-Diego: "Playa San Diego in Costa del Balsamo is an exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf Offshore winds blow from the north northeast. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the south southwest. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of the strong rips here." Access (surfnerd): Access is easy: turn off the main coastal highway and follow the smaller roads down to the beach. facts.name: Popoyo
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Popoyo is one of Nicaragua's classic, most consistent reef setups, breaking over a flat slab of rock reef and sand at the southern end of Playa Guasacate. The peak throws both lefts and rights with real speed and plenty of open face, giving you room to carve and whack to your heart's content. It's often likened to Lower Trestles, and on its day it ranks among the best, most rippable waves in the country. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Access (surfnerd): Park at the south end of town using the free roadside parking, and leave nothing of value in the car, then cross the rivermouth to reach the break. There's a surf school in the area if you want a hand getting started.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Popoyo Outer Reef is a heaving left slab that breaks over rock and lava a quarter-mile outside the far friendlier Popoyo Main Reef. Imagine The Box in Australia flipped around, given a gnarly end-section and asked to hold solid 20-foot surf, and you're close. It's one of the best and few genuine big-wave spots in Central America, and it stays sketchy even on its better days. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Popoyo: "Popoyo in Tola Province is an exposed reef break that has very consistent waves Offshore winds are from the northeast. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Sometimes crowded. Take care of - Rips / undertow - Rocks." Access (surfnerd): Park at the very south end of the one road leading into Popoyo, then walk across the rivermouth to the south. You can't miss it. Coming in by boat is the other option. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Potrero Grande, better known as Ollie's Point, is a long right-hand pointbreak on Costa Rica's Pacific coast near the Nicaraguan border. Perfectly tapered rights peel down the point over uneven reef and sand, and the walls run long and forgiving, giving you room to work on your surfing as a session unfolds. Made famous in "Endless Summer II", this rivermouth point rates among the more enjoyable rights around. Getting there is part of the deal: the only way in is by boat. Check: surfnerd states facing SSE but best swell W (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Potrero-Grande: "Potrero Grande(OlliesPoint) in Guanacaste is an exposed point/Rivermouth break that has consistent surf Ideal winds are from the northeast. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southwest. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Hazards include rocks, sharks,sea crcodiles,sea-lice and isolation." Access (surfnerd): The only way in is by boat, a long trip up the coast from Playas del Coco, and parking on the mainland is restricted. Because it's so remote, keep in mind that medical help is a long way off. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Potrero-Grande 0.5 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Puerto Sandino is a long left that peels over a mix of uneven reef and sand, and it ranks among Nicaragua's best and longest waves, with rides reaching up to 400 metres when the sandbars line up. It breaks out in the open at a large rivermouth, almost half a mile from shore, so it feels exposed and picks up more swell than the nearby breaks. Take-offs can be fast and steep, feeding into a string of barrel and wall sections broken up along the way. Check: surfnerd states facing WNW but best swell SW (67.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Puerto-Sandino: "Puerto Sandino in Leon Province is an exposed reef and point break that has quite reliable surf The best wind direction is from the northeast. Clean groundswells prevail and the best swell direction is from the southwest. There are left and right breaking reefs. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Boat access is the way to go here, and most surfers reach the wave that way. You can paddle from shore, but it's a long haul across strong currents. Parking nearby is restricted, and with the wave sitting in a rivermouth, keep an eye out for debris flushing out of the river. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Puerto-Sandino 0.7 km.

It tends to be bigger here than anywhere else nearby, so it is often safer to surf from a boat and steer clear of getting caught inside. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. A fairly popluar wave that can sometimes get crowded Beware of urchins and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Surf camps are strung along the cliffs above, with camping and a surf school close by. Parking is restricted. If you are tackling it from land rather than by boat, booties are essential over the rocky reef. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Punta-Brava 1.3 km.

Expect fast inside runners and tubes on the inside sections at higher tides, and when the swell cranks, the outside turns on for heavier, hollow rides. The paddle out is easy, though long rides on bigger days mean longer paddles back.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Punta Roca is a world-class right-hand point that peels over black boulders for nearly half a mile, throwing up steep walls, multiple barrel sections, and long open faces. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Punta Uvita is a whale-tail-shaped point that serves as the gateway to Marino Ballena, one of only two marine parks in Costa Rica. facts.name: Quepos Jetty

facts.tide: Low (Best at Low, Better on rising) (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Quepos Jetty is a left-hander that breaks over sand at the rivermouth. The original wave used to peel point-like into the estuary, and when the large Pez Vela marina went in, everyone assumed that was the end of it. Instead, the new harbour wall and the river's exit point have combined to build an even better version of the wave. How it behaves depends almost entirely on size. At waist to chest high it's mushy and slow, which suits longboards. Anything bigger and it peels extremely fast, with barrel sections on the inside and no room to fit a cutback in. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): There are restrooms, and parking runs from a free car park to paid and roadside options. Wear ear plugs, as the water gets polluted after rain, and keep an eye out for the heavy boat traffic.

It is best known for the length of its rides: depending on the swell direction, waves run 200 to 400 metres down either side of the triangle, breaking both left and right. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Silverbacks is Bocas del Toro's big-wave spot and the only right-hand reefbreak in the zone, sitting off Bastimientos and breaking over coral. It stays docile for most of the year, then thumps its chest through the winter months. When it turns on, it sucks up huge volumes of water and hurls them at a shallow ledge, throwing large, intense kegs that are as short as they are heavy. The menacing name fits a muscular, angry wave. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Silverbacks: "Silverbacks in Bocas del Torro is an exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf The best wind direction is from the southwest. Waves more likely to be from local windswells than distant groundswells and the ideal wave direction is from the northeast. A right hand reef. Surfable at all stages of the tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Beware of rocks, rips etc." Access (surfnerd): Getting there means a 20-minute boat ride from town, and it is not a trip for casual surfers. Parking on shore is restricted. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Silverbacks 1.4 km.

facts.name: Sunzal
facts.windOffshore: N (surfnerd wind exposure NW - NE, "Offshore from N"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Sunzal is a long right-hand point that peels over a broad boulder reef, one of the most dependable waves on El Salvador's coast. The reef juts well out to sea, so it pulls in almost any swell that's running, and the sharply angled, relatively deep setup holds its shape in all but the biggest days. The trade-off is a soft, forgiving wave with plenty of fat sections and long rides. If it's flat at Sunzal, it's flat everywhere. The break sits just up the coast from El Tunco, a laid-back village at the river mouth. Overall it's a decent, fun wave rather than a textbook point. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): You'll find a surf shop at the spot, plus a car park with free parking and roadside spots nearby. You can also reach it by bus from La Libertad in about half an hour for less than a dollar. Take care getting in and out when the surf has size and the tide is high, as it can get a bit sketchy.

facts.name: Tamarindo
facts.facing: NW (surfnerd tamarindo-provincia-de-guanacaste: "Faces NW"); WNW (surfnerd tamarindo: "Faces WNW")
facts.swellExposure: WSW to W, W to NNW (surfnerd)
facts.windOffshore: SE (surfnerd wind exposure E - S, "Offshore from SE"); East (surf-forecast)
hazards: Local Tips Expect a very busy lineup across the bay, and heavy crowds are the main hazard here. (surfnerd)
facts.season: Spring, Summer (surfnerd); Winter, most often January (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Tamarindo is a four-mile bay in Guanacaste with at least four distinct breaks strung along it, so the name covers a stretch of coast rather than a single peak. Waves break over sand and rock, and you'll find both rights and lefts depending on where you paddle out. Overall it's a decent, fun setup with something for most surfers. From north to south, Playa Grande is the most consistent of the bunch: a cooking beachbreak that tends to close out at low tide but delivers near-shore A-frame tubes from mid to high. It's always bigger than in town, and when everything else is flat, Grande will still have something to ride. It's at its best when an off-season south swell lines up with wintertime offshores. El Estero, the Tamarindo Rivermouth, isn't a classic rivermouth setup, but when the sand settles right, which it can for weeks at a time, it's a good wave, with rights on the south side and lefts on the north. Tamarindo Beachbreak is an average wave that never matches Playa Grande, but it sits right in town and draws plenty of beginners. Pico Pequeno is a right lava reefbreak that can get really good; it seems to favour a southwest swell and a mid to high tide, since low is sketchy and shallow, and being a one-peak wave makes the crowd especially difficult. Surfnerd has 2 entries for this break with different stated facings (tamarindo-provincia-de-guanacaste=NW, tamarindo=WNW); seaward uses the primary entry (tamarindo-provincia-de-guanacaste), both kept. Second Surfnerd entry https://www.surfnerd.com/surf-forecast/tamarindo: workable swell SW - NW (Best from NW), 2ft - 7ft, Sand, Beach, Left, Right, Mid, High, Beginner. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Tamarindo: "Tamarindo in Guanacaste is an exposed beach break that has consistent surf Offshore winds are from the east. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the west northwest. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. It's often crowded here. Beware of ." Access (surfnerd): The Tamarindo spots are all in town and easy to reach on foot. Playa Grande sits further north and takes a drive or a hike to get to. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Tamarindo 0.8 km, surfnerd tamarindo 0.4 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: The Boom is a world-class A-frame beachbreak in Northern Nicaragua, and the hollow, dredging, backdrafting peaks it throws are why people keep coming back. It has been likened to a miniature Puerto Escondido: shifting sandbars, plenty of rip, startling consistency, and an outside canyon that pulls swell straight to the beach. The break splits into three zones, with Coconuts to the north, Powder Puffs to the south, and The Boom proper in the middle. It was pioneered in the late 1990s by Miami expat Shay O'Brien, who founded Chancletas Beach Resort with his wife Loretta and their three daughters in 2003. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate, Expert. Access (surfnerd): Roll onto the beach with a 4x4 or a motorcycle, or stay at Chancletas and stroll down the path a few times a day. Don't forget your sandals.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Tivives is a beachbreak that closes out easily, so the waves to look for are the rights that run into the rivermouth and the Mini Valor lefts that peel off the point. It breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand and holds both lefts and rights, though the wrapping swells favour the lefts, with the occasional right showing up at Valor. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Tavives: "Tavives in Golfo de Nicoya is a fairly exposed beach break that does not work very often The best wind direction is from the northeast. Clean groundswells prevail and the best swell direction is from the southwest. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Sometimes crowded. Beware of rips and polluition." Access (surfnerd): There's free roadside parking. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Tavives 1.5 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Toro de Oro is a right-hand point that peels over a mix of uneven reef and sand. It serves up fast, long rides that only the best surfers will make clean, though from the side it can look deceptively inviting. When it comes together, the wave breaks consistently. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Access (surfnerd): Toro de Oro is best reached by boat, thanks to a rugged volcanic rock shoreline that makes paddling out from the beach a tough proposition.

facts.name: Tortuguero Beach
facts.windOffshore: WSW (surfnerd wind exposure SSW - WNW, "Offshore from WSW"); SW (surfnerd guide text: "southwest (SW) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Tortuguero Beach is a sand-bottomed beachbreak on Costa Rica's Caribbean side, part of the vast Tortuguero National Park where the beaches run for mile after remote mile. It picks up both lefts and rights, and the easiest way in is by boat from Puerto Moin, which also opens up the northern breaks around Parismina and Barra Colorado. Expect average, everyday waves rather than anything world-class, but there's plenty of empty sand to yourself. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): Getting here takes some effort: a boat from Puerto Moin is the usual route, and you can also walk in from the jetty at Playa Main to get a look at conditions first. There's a surf shop in the area, plus free roadside parking. The water near the rivermouths can run brown and murky, so it pays to pick your spot along the beach.

facts.facing: SW (surfnerd witches-rock: "Faces SW"); SW (surfnerd witches-rock-roca-bruja: "Faces SW")
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); East (surf-forecast)

facts.season: Spring, Summer, Winter (surfnerd); Winter, most often January (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Witches Rock is an easy, playful beachbreak on the white-sand stretch of Playa Naranjo, breaking over sand and producing both lefts and rights. The estuary drops sand onto an otherwise fairly flat sandbar, and that's what builds the walls here: long, groomed, green lines that hold up without necessarily closing out. Other peaks run along the two to three-mile beach, but the ones tucked in the lee of the rock are the best shaped of the bunch. When it lines up, it's genuinely fun surfing. Surfnerd lists this break 2 times (witches-rock, witches-rock-roca-bruja); merged. Second Surfnerd entry https://www.surfnerd.com/surf-forecast/witches-rock-roca-bruja: workable swell S - W (Best from SW), 4ft - 12ft, Sand, Beach, Left, Right, Mid, High, Beginner. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Surf-forecast Roca-Bruja: "Roca Bruja in Guanacaste is an exposed beach break that has consistent surf Works best in offshore winds from the east. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell direction is from the west northwest. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Rarely crowded here. Watch out for sharks." Access (surfnerd): Getting there is either a rough drive or a comfortable boat taxi. Take your pick. The water itself is clean. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Roca-Bruja 0.9 km, surfnerd witches-rock-roca-bruja 0.4 km.

facts.name: Zancudo
facts.windOffshore: ENE (surfnerd wind exposure NNE - ESE, "Offshore from ENE"); E (surfnerd guide text: "east (E) offshore wind"); Northeast (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid, High (surfnerd); Best around mid tide. (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Zancudo is a sand-bottomed beach break tucked far inside the Golfo Dulce, right by a large rivermouth. It is better known for great fishing than for surfing, but the mellow waves and reasonably priced beachfront accommodation make it a comfortable place for new surfers to log some water time. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Zancudo: "Zancudo in Golfo Dulce is a sheltered point break that has reasonably consistent surf Works best in offshore winds from the northeast. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southwest.The waves is a point break that peels left. Best around mid tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of Jellyfish,sea-lice." Access (surfnerd): There is camping close by, and parking is free, either roadside or nearby. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Zancudo 3.4 km.
